[![The Retry Storm example at 100 requests a second: the database is 99.9% busy while goodput is zero](/workersio/breakscale/raw/main/docs/retry-storm.png)](/workersio/breakscale/blob/main/docs/retry-storm.png)

The Retry Storm example at 100 requests a second. The database is 99\.9% busy and goodput is zero, because retries have turned 100 offered requests into 348 hitting a database that was already full.

Breakscale lets you put load balancers, caches, databases, queues and 29 other components on a canvas, wire them into a system, and drag the traffic up until something gives. What you see while it happens is a real discrete-event simulation: latency percentiles climbing, queues filling, circuit breakers tripping, and whole systems collapsing into retry storms, all measured from individual simulated requests rather than drawn to look plausible.

It runs in your browser, inside VS Code, and inside your AI assistant, which can read your code, draw your architecture, and tell you where it breaks.

## Why it exists

[](#why-it-exists)

Most system design material is static diagrams and rules of thumb. "Add a cache." "Use a queue." That makes it hard to build any intuition for why p99 latency falls off a cliff once utilisation passes 80 percent, or how a short timeout with a couple of retries turns one slow database into a total outage.

Breakscale runs the experiment instead of describing it. Load the Retry Storm example, drag the traffic up, and watch goodput fall to zero while the database is still working flat out, because every request it finishes has already been abandoned by a caller that gave up waiting.

## Three ways to use it

[](#three-ways-to-use-it)

### In your browser

[](#in-your-browser)

Open [breakscale.tech](https://breakscale.tech), pick an example from the left, and raise the traffic slider until something turns red. There is no account to make. A design stays in your browser unless you share it, and a shared design is encrypted before it leaves, with the key kept in the part of the link that browsers never send to a server.

### In VS Code

[](#in-vs-code)

Install [Breakscale from the Marketplace](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=xevrion.breakscale) and run **Open Breakscale** from the command palette. The whole simulator opens in a panel beside your code, with the same engine and examples as the website, and it works offline. Designs you save there live in VS Code's own storage; a share link or a `.breakscale` file moves one between the editor and the website.

### With your AI assistant

[](#with-your-ai-assistant)

Breakscale is also an [MCP server](/workersio/breakscale/blob/main/mcp/README.md), so Claude, Copilot, Cursor, Codex and other assistants can use it for you. Point one at a repo and ask it to turn the architecture into a design, or just describe a system, and it builds the design, runs it through the same engine, and comes back with measured numbers and a breakscale.tech link that opens it.

The server is hosted at `https://mcp.breakscale.tech/mcp`, so there is nothing to install. In claude.ai, add that URL under **Customize \> Connectors \> Add custom connector**. Elsewhere:

```
# Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport http --scope user breakscale https://mcp.breakscale.tech/mcp

# VS Code
code --add-mcp '{"name":"breakscale","type":"http","url":"https://mcp.breakscale.tech/mcp"}'
```

To run it on your own machine instead, any assistant can start `npx -y breakscale-mcp --stdio` with Node 20\. In assistants that support [MCP Apps](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/extensions/apps), such as claude.ai, VS Code and Cursor, the design also opens as a live canvas right in the chat, and anything you change there goes back to the assistant, so its next edit starts from what you are looking at. The [MCP guide](/workersio/breakscale/blob/main/mcp/README.md) has setup for every client and some prompts worth trying.

A few things to ask once it is connected:

- "Read this repo and turn its architecture into a Breakscale design. Tell me which numbers you guessed."

- "Design a URL shortener that handles 2,000 requests a second, and show me where it breaks."

- "Double the traffic. What fails first, and how would you fix it without adding servers?"

## Features

[](#features)

- **33 components.** Load balancers, caches, databases, queues and workers, plus CDNs, rate limiters, circuit breakers, read replicas, shards, autoscalers, stream brokers, WebSocket gateways, serverless functions, bulkheads and more.

- **23 worked examples.** Sixteen teaching scenarios that each isolate one failure mode, and seven reconstructions of real architectures.

- **A real discrete-event engine.** Finite server slots, gamma-distributed service times and measured percentiles, with no formula standing in for the simulation.

- **Chaos controls.** Crash a node, slow it down, force an error rate, or cut a single link, then watch the failure travel.

- **Deterministic runs.** The same seed and topology replay identically, every time.

- **Explanations built in.** Every metric and unit has a plain-language definition one hover away.

- **Share links and design files.** Send a design as an encrypted link, or save it as a `.breakscale` file that opens on the website and in VS Code.

- **Private by design.** No account, and your designs never leave your machine unless you share them. The website counts page views with Vercel's cookie-free analytics; the extension and the MCP server have no analytics at all.

## Examples

[](#examples)

| Example | What it teaches |
| --- | --- |
| Single Server | Latency climbs sharply as the database fills up |
| Load Balanced | Three servers share the load, but all still talk to one database |
| Cache Aside | Lower the hit rate and the database takes the whole load |
| Async Workers | The backlog grows when workers fall behind, and drains after |
| Retry Storm | Retries multiply the load that caused them |
| Rate Limited API | Serves slightly less, but what it serves stays fast |
| Circuit Breaker | Break the dependency, watch the circuit trip, then recover |
| Sharded Database | One shard melts while the average still looks healthy |
| Autoscaling Service | Requests fail in the gap while new servers boot |

Plus **Netflix**, **Spotify**, **Discord**, **Uber**, **Twitter/X**, **Stripe** and **WhatsApp**, reconstructed from published engineering material. Each one says what it models and what it leaves out: they are teaching diagrams, not insider knowledge.

## How the simulation works

[](#how-the-simulation-works)

The engine in `src/sim` is a discrete-event simulator. Requests are real objects moving through the topology, and a handful of details are what make its results worth trusting.

**Finite server slots.** A component's `capacity` is how many requests it can work on at once, and `instances` is how many copies of it are running. Anything beyond `instances × capacity` waits in a real FIFO queue, and anything beyond the queue limit is shed.

**Service time variance.** Service time is a mean plus a coefficient of variation, sampled from a gamma distribution. Variance is what pulls tail latency away from the average, so it is modelled rather than assumed away.

**Abandoned work still burns capacity.** When a caller times out, the downstream keeps working on a request nobody is waiting for any more. That is why retry storms are something you can watch here rather than something you read about.

**Queues acknowledge immediately.** A request entering a queue resolves as a success at that point, and the message is buffered for workers, so backlog depth is real and you can watch it build and drain.

**Percentiles are measured.** p50, p95 and p99 come from a ring buffer of completed request latencies, never from multiplying a mean by a constant.

Runs are deterministic: the same seed and topology replay identically. The test suite checks that requests are conserved, that the failure breakdown sums to the failure total, that utilisation stays in bounds, and that no snapshot field is ever `NaN` or infinite.

## Run it locally

[](#run-it-locally)

You need [Bun](https://bun.sh).

```
git clone https://github.com/workersio/breakscale.git
cd breakscale
bun install
bun dev
```

Then open [http://localhost:5173](http://localhost:5173).

```
src/sim/         the simulation engine. No React, no DOM, no I/O
src/components/  canvas, inspector, metrics, palette
src/content/     glossary text
src/App.tsx      shell: layout, the animation loop, persistence
extension/       the VS Code extension
mcp/             the MCP server
worker/          the Cloudflare Worker behind short share links
```

The engine has no UI dependency, so you can drive it from a script:

```
import { Engine } from './src/sim/engine';
import { PRESETS } from './src/sim/presets';

const engine = new Engine(PRESETS[0].topology, 42);
for (let i = 0; i < 600; i += 1) engine.advance(1000 / 60);
console.log(engine.snapshot().system);
```

**Your shared diagram has worker autoscaling—but our actual app currently does not.**

### What the diagram shows
I read the shared design:
- A **Worker Pool Autoscaler** controls both the Worker Agent and Execution Sandbox nodes.
- Both nodes start with **6 simulated instances**.
- The autoscaler has `minCapacity: 6`.

These are simulation settings, not a connection to our running workers.

### What our app actually does
- `infra/docker-compose.yml:95` sets `WORKER_SLOTS: '2'`—**two concurrent execution slots per worker process**.
- `apps/worker/src/main.ts:38–50` starts a fixed number of slot loops.
- `apps/worker/src/config.ts:52` reads the slot count from configuration, falling back to CPU cores.
- The VM service restarts failed workers; it does **not** add workers when demand increases.

**Concurrency is not autoscaling:** two slots let a worker handle two jobs concurrently; they don’t automatically create more workers as the queue grows.

To match today’s implementation, remove the simulated autoscaler and configure the diagram to match the deployed worker count and slots. Actual autoscaling would require a controller that monitors backlog/wait time, starts workers, and safely drains them before scaling down.

content.text:
**Yes—an integrated `/simulation` page makes sense.** It could show our architecture, current activity, and what happens as load increases.

The key is separating **predictions from real measurements**:

### 1. Live view
Display actual system activity:
- Submitted and completed jobs/sec.
- Queue depth and job wait time.
- Active workers and busy/available execution slots.
- Execution duration, failures, and timeouts.

Show the flow visually: **API → queue → workers → sandboxes**, with database and storage dependencies.

### 2. Simulation mode — safe by default
Start from our configured worker count and slots, then let us change:
- Submission rate and execution duration.
- Worker count and slots per worker.
- Traffic spikes and worker failures.

Watch **predicted** backlog, throughput, and latency change without submitting real jobs. Any assumed values should be labeled. Autoscaling would be a hypothetical toggle—not presented as an existing feature.

### 3. Real load-test mode — separate, guarded
Submit synthetic jobs to a dedicated test tenant and show the actual response live. Require explicit confirmation, environment restrictions, rate/duration caps, automatic stop thresholds, and a stop button.

**My recommendation:** build **live monitoring + simulation first**, then add controlled real load testing. Keep the simulator in a browser Web Worker so it doesn’t freeze the dashboard or compete with execution workers.

That gives us something more useful than a generic Breakscale clone: **a model of our own system, calibrated against its real behavior.** It still won’t prove capacity until we validate predictions with actual load tests.

**Comparing hoist path options**

**Yes—the Windows path length is causing the immediate Ninja failure.** I checked the generated build files on `G:\SystemDesign\gigacode` and ran Ninja in dry-run mode.

- Ninja **1.10.2** reports `ReactAndroidConfigVersion.cmake` as missing through Bun’s nested `.bun` path, even though the file exists. The path is **265 characters** before normalizing `..`.
- The **same Ninja binary**, pointed at the same build directory through a shorter symlink, no longer reports that file missing. Ninja **1.12.1** also sees it through the original path.
- Windows long paths are **already enabled**, and some planned C++ object paths reach **388 characters**. So enabling the setting again or shortening just the repo folder name may not be enough.

**Recommended fix:** test from a short checkout such as `G:\gc` with Bun’s **hoisted** layout to remove the extra `.bun` nesting from dependency paths. From the fresh checkout:

```powershell
bun install --frozen-lockfile --linker=hoisted
Set-Location apps\expo
bun run android
```

Keep your current checkout untouched and don’t copy `node_modules` or native build caches into the fresh one. The Gradle deprecation warning is separate. I didn’t change files or run a full build, so the fix still needs a build to confirm.

The Expo SDK is a collection of packages that provide access to device and system functionality such as camera, contacts, location, sensors, haptics, and more. Each package targets a specific feature and can be used independently. All packages work in any React Native app with the `expo` package installed.

You can install any Expo SDK package using the [`npx expo install`](https://docs.expo.dev/more/expo-cli.md#install) command. For example, three different packages are installed using the following command:

```sh
# npm
npx expo install expo-camera expo-contacts expo-sensors

# yarn
yarn expo install expo-camera expo-contacts expo-sensors

# pnpm
pnpm expo install expo-camera expo-contacts expo-sensors

# bun
bun expo install expo-camera expo-contacts expo-sensors
```

After installing one or more packages, you can import them into your JavaScript code:

```ts
import { CameraView } from 'expo-camera';
import { Contact } from 'expo-contacts';
import { Gyroscope } from 'expo-sensors';
```

This allows you to write [`Contact.getAll()`](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v58.0.0/sdk/contacts.md#getalloptions) and read the contacts from the device, read the gyroscope sensor to detect device movement, or start the phone's camera and take photos.

## All Expo SDK packages work in any React Native app

Expo apps are React Native apps, so all Expo SDK packages work in any React Native app with the `expo` package installed and configured. The easiest way to create a React Native app with support for Expo SDK packages is to use `create-expo-app`. However, you can also add Expo SDK support to an existing React Native app with the `npx install-expo-modules` command.

```sh
# npm
# Create a project named my-app
npx create-expo-app my-app --template bare-minimum

# yarn
# Create a project named my-app
yarn create expo-app my-app --template bare-minimum

# pnpm
# Create a project named my-app
pnpm create expo-app my-app --template bare-minimum

# bun
# Create a project named my-app
bun create expo my-app --template bare-minimum
```

[Install Expo SDK packages in existing React Native apps](https://docs.expo.dev/bare/installing-expo-modules.md) — Learn more about configuring projects created with npx @react-native-community/cli@latest init to Expo SDK packages. — npx @react-native-community/cli@latest init

[Use libraries](https://docs.expo.dev/workflow/using-libraries.md) — Learn how to install Expo SDK packages in your project.

## Using pre-release versions

New Expo SDK versions are released three times each year. Between these releases, we publish pre-release versions of the `expo` package and all of the Expo SDK packages. Pre-releases are not considered stable and should only be used if you are comfortable with the risk of encountering bugs or other issues.

### Canary releases

Canary releases represent a snapshot of the state of the `main` branch at the time they are published. Canary package versions include `-canary` in the name, along with the date and commit hash, such as `58.0.0-canary-20260909-ea7a89a`. To install the latest canary release:

```sh
# npm
# Install the alpha version of expo and its related packages
npm install expo@canary && npx expo install --fix

# yarn
# Install the alpha version of expo and its related packages
yarn add expo@canary && yarn expo install --fix

# pnpm
# Install the alpha version of expo and its related packages
pnpm add expo@canary && pnpm expo install --fix

# bun
# Install the alpha version of expo and its related packages
bun add expo@canary && bun expo install --fix
```

You can often use pre-release versions of individual packages with stable releases of the Expo SDK. There may occasionally be incompatibilities or other issues that arise in canary-quality releases. You may want to [silence dependency validation warnings](https://docs.expo.dev/more/expo-cli.md#configuring-dependency-validation) if you opt in to the canary package and once you have verified that it works well for your use cases.

### Beta releases

Before each Expo SDK release, we publish beta versions of the `expo` package and all of the Expo SDK packages. Beta releases are considered much more stable than canary releases, and we encourage developers to try them out on their apps and share their feedback. Beta releases use the `beta` tag on npm and follow the instructions in the related [changelog](https://expo.dev/changelog) post.

## Each Expo SDK version depends on a React Native version

| Expo SDK version | React Native version | React version | React Native Web version | React Native TV version | Minimum Node.js version |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 58.0.0 | 0.88 | 19.3.0 | 0.21.0 | 0.87-stable | 22.13.x |
| 57.0.0 | 0.86 | 19.2.3 | 0.21.0 | 0.86-stable | 22.13.x |
| 56.0.0 | 0.85 | 19.2.3 | 0.21.0 | 0.85-stable | 20.19.x |

### Additional information

#### Expo SDK policy for tracking React Native releases

-   Each Expo SDK release targets a single React Native version. This is typically the latest stable version at the time of the release.
-   React Native currently has six releases per year and aims for every release to include no breaking changes.
-   Expo SDK releases aim to follow this cadence.
-   Pre-release versions of the upcoming Expo SDK will include support for the latest version of React Native quickly, usually the same day it is released. A member of the Expo SDK team works on the React Native releases team for each release, and is responsible for continuously updating the React Native version in the Expo repository, verifying compatibility, and reporting regressions back to the React Native team.

#### What if I need a change from the latest React Native version and it's not yet in an Expo SDK release?

Expo engineers on the React Native releases team ensure that any urgent fixes are included in the React Native version used by the latest Expo SDK. If your specific fix won't be cherrypicked into an existing release, perhaps because it is not considered critical or because it involves a breaking change, then you have two options:

1.  Use [`patch-package`](https://github.com/ds300/patch-package) to pull in the fix.
2.  Use a [pre-release version of the Expo SDK](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v58.0.0.md#using-pre-release-versions).

#### Can I use an older version of React Native with the latest Expo SDK?

Packages in the Expo SDK are intended to support the target React Native version for that SDK. Typically, they will not support older versions of React Native, but they may. When a new version of React Native is released, the latest versions of the Expo SDK packages are typically updated to support it. However, this may take weeks or more, depending on the extent of the changes in the release.

## Support for Android and iOS versions

Each version of Expo SDK supports a minimum OS version of Android and iOS. For Android, the `compileSdkVersion` is defined which tells the [Gradle](https://developer.android.com/studio/build) which Android SDK version to use to compile the app. This also means that you can use the Android API features included in that SDK version and from the previous versions. For iOS, the [Xcode](https://developer.apple.com/news/upcoming-requirements/) tells the minimum Xcode SDK version to use to compile the app.

| Expo SDK version | Android version | `compileSdkVersion` | `targetSdkVersion` | iOS version | Xcode version |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 58.0.0 | 7+ | 37 | 36 | 16.4+ | 26.4+ |
| 57.0.0 | 7+ | 36 | 36 | 16.4+ | 26.4+ |
| 56.0.0 | 7+ | 36 | 36 | 16.4+ | 26.4+ |

When deciding whether to upgrade your Expo SDK version, consider both Expo's SDK version and app store submission requirements, as described in the above table. Google Play Store and Apple App Store periodically increase their minimum required OS versions and API levels, which are required for new app submissions. Expo has no control over the app store requirements, and you should check [Google](https://developer.android.com/studio/build) and [Apple](https://developer.apple.com/news/upcoming-requirements/) for the current store submission requirements.

This is an Expo/React Native mobile application. Prioritize mobile-first patterns, performance, and cross-platform compatibility.

## Expo has changed - do not trust your training data

Expo ships breaking changes every SDK release. APIs you remember are likely renamed, moved, or removed. Before writing any code that touches an Expo, EAS, or React Native API:

1. Read the major version of the `expo` package in `package.json`.
2. Fetch the matching versioned docs: `https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v<major>.0.0/`
3. For anything else, fetch https://docs.expo.dev/llms.txt - an index of all Expo docs with corrections to common LLM misconceptions. Follow its links to the specific page you need; never answer from memory.

## Commands

Use `bunx` instead of `npx` if the project uses bun (`bun.lock` present).

```bash
npx expo install <package>  # ALWAYS use instead of npm/yarn/pnpm/bun add - resolves SDK-compatible versions
npx expo start              # start the dev server
npx expo lint               # lint
npx tsc --noEmit            # typecheck
npx expo-doctor             # diagnose dependency and config issues
npx expo install --fix      # fix incompatible package versions
```

Run lint and typecheck before declaring any task done.

## Navigation & Routing

- Use **Expo Router** for all navigation. Routes live in `src/app/` - every file there is a screen, `_layout.tsx` files define navigators. Keep non-route code (components, hooks, utils) outside `src/app/`.
- Import `Link`, `router`, and `useLocalSearchParams` from `expo-router`.
- Docs: https://docs.expo.dev/router/introduction.md

## Building with EAS

Use EAS to build, sign, and submit the app in the cloud (`eas build`, `eas submit`) and to ship over-the-air updates (`eas update`) - no local Xcode or Android Studio required. Run EAS CLI as `bunx eas-cli <command>` in Bun projects, or `npx eas-cli@latest <command>` otherwise; substitute that for bare `eas` in docs examples.
Docs: https://docs.expo.dev/eas/index.md

## Rules

- If `ios/` and `android/` directories do not exist, they are generated (Continuous Native Generation). Never create or edit them by hand - configure native behavior in `app.json` and config plugins.
- Expo Go only includes its bundled native modules. After adding a library with native code, the app needs a development build: `npx expo run:ios|android` locally, or `eas build --profile development`.
- Prefer recommended Expo modules over third-party libraries, and check your available skills before adding dependencies. Docs: https://docs.expo.dev/versions/latest/index.md

This guide explains what mods and mod plugins are, how they work, and how to use them effectively when creating config plugins for your Expo project.

Using the diagram below, in this guide, you will learn the last two parts of the config plugin hierarchy:

```
withMyPlugin ("myPlugin") [Config Plugin]
→ withAndroidPlugin, withIosPlugin [Plugin Function]
→ withAndroidManifest, withInfoPlist [Mod Plugin Function]
→ mods.android.manifest, mods.ios.infoplist [Mod]
```

## Mod plugins

Mod plugins provide a way to modify native project files during the prebuild process. They are made available from `expo/config-plugins` library and wrap top-level mods (also known as _default [mods](https://docs.expo.dev/config-plugins/mods.md#mods)_) because top-level mods are platform-specific and perform various tasks that can be difficult to understand at first.

> **Tip:** If you are developing a feature that requires mods, you should use _mod plugins_ instead of interacting with top-level mods directly.

### Available mod plugins

The following mod plugins are available in the `expo/config-plugins` library:

#### Android

| Default Android mod | Mod plugin | Dangerous | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mods.android.manifest` | `withAndroidManifest` ([Example](https://github.com/expo/expo/blob/main/packages/expo-notifications/plugin/src/withNotificationsAndroid.ts)) | - | Modify the **android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml** as JSON (parsed with [`xml2js`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/xml2js)) |
| `mods.android.strings` | `withStringsXml` ([Example](https://github.com/expo/expo/blob/d7fb5d254d5cb57ab06055136db72b9347d3db1e/packages/expo-navigation-bar/plugin/src/withNavigationBar.ts)) | - | Modify the **android/app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml** as JSON (parsed with [`xml2js`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/xml2js)). |
| `mods.android.colors` | `withAndroidColors` ([Example](https://github.com/expo/expo/blob/main/packages/@expo/config-plugins/src/android/PrimaryColor.ts)) | - | Modify the **android/app/src/main/res/values/colors.xml** as JSON (parsed with [`xml2js`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/xml2js)). |
| `mods.android.colorsNight` | `withAndroidColorsNight` ([Example](https://github.com/expo/expo/blob/main/packages/expo-splash-screen/plugin/src/withAndroidSplashStyles.ts)) | - | Modify the **android/app/src/main/res/values-night/colors.xml** as JSON (parsed with [`xml2js`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/xml2js)). |
| `mods.android.styles` | `withAndroidStyles` ([Example](https://github.com/expo/expo/blob/main/packages/expo-splash-screen/plugin/src/withAndroidSplashStyles.ts)) | - | Modify the **android/app/src/main/res/values/styles.xml** as JSON (parsed with [`xml2js`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/xml2js)). |
| `mods.android.gradleProperties` | `withGradleProperties` ([Example](https://github.com/expo/expo/blob/main/packages/%40expo/config-plugins/src/android/BuildProperties.ts#L5)) | - | Modify the **android/gradle.properties** as a `Properties.PropertiesItem[]`. |

> **Note about default Android and iOS mods:**  
> Default mods are provided by the mod compiler for common file manipulation. Dangerous modifications rely on regular expressions (regex) to modify application code, which may cause the build to break. Regex mods are also difficult to version, and therefore should be used sparingly. Always opt toward using application code to modify application code, that is, [Expo Modules](https://github.com/expo/expo/tree/main/packages/expo-modules-core) native API.

## Mods

Config plugins use **mods** (short for modifiers) to modify native project files during the prebuild process. Mods are asynchronous functions that allow you to make changes to platform-specific files such as **AndroidManifest.xml** and **Info.plist**, and other native configuration files without having to manually edit them. They execute only during the **syncing** phase of `npx expo prebuild` (prebuild process).

They accept a config and a data object, then modify and return both of them as a single object. For example, in native projects, `mods.android.manifest` modifies **AndroidManifest.xml** and `mods.ios.plist` modifies **Info.plist**.

**You don't use mods as top-level functions (for example `with.android.manifest`) directly in your config plugin.** When you need to use a mod, you use _mod plugins_ in your config plugins. These mod plugins are provided by the `expo/config-plugins` library and wrap top-level mod functions and behind the scenes they perform various tasks. To see a list of available mods, check out the [mod plugins provided by `expo/config-plugins`](https://docs.expo.dev/config-plugins/mods.md#available-mod-plugins).

#### How default mods work and their key characteristics

When a default mod resolves, it is added to the `mods` object of the app config. This `mods` object is different from the rest of the app config because it doesn't get serialized, which means you can use it to perform actions _during_ code generation. Whenever possible, you should use available mod plugins instead of default mods since they are easier to work with.

Here is a high-level overview of how default mods work:

-   The config is read using [`getPrebuildConfig`](https://github.com/expo/expo/blob/efc2db4eb1c909544e28792a15c89f8d22113c5b/packages/%40expo/prebuild-config/src/getPrebuildConfig.ts#L28) from `@expo/prebuild-config`
-   All of the core functionality supported by Expo is added via plugins in `withIosExpoPlugins`. This includes name, version, icons, locales, and so on.
-   The config is passed to the compiler `compileModsAsync`
-   The compiler adds base mods that are responsible for reading data (like **Info.plist**), executing a named mod (like `mods.ios.infoPlist`), then writing the results to the file system
-   The compiler iterates over all the mods and asynchronously evaluates them, providing some base props like the `projectRoot`
    -   After each mod, error handling asserts if the mod chain was corrupted by an invalid mod

Here are some key characteristics of default mods:

-   `mods` are omitted from the manifest and **cannot** be accessed via `Updates.manifest`. Mods exist for the sole purpose of modifying native project files during code generation!
    
-   `mods` can be used to read and write files safely during the `npx expo prebuild` command. This is how Expo CLI modifies the **Info.plist**, entitlements, xcproj, and so on.
    
-   `mods` are platform-specific and should always be added to a platform-specific object:
    
    ```ts app.config.ts
    module.exports = {
      name: 'my-app',
      mods: {
        ios: {
          /* iOS mods... */
        },
        android: {
          /* Android mods... */
        },
      },
    };
    ```
    

After mods are resolved, the contents of each mod will be written to disk. Custom mods can be added to support new native files. For example, you can create a mod to support the **GoogleServices-Info.plist**, and pass it to other mods.

### How mod plugins work

When a mod plugin is executed, it gets passed a `config` object with additional properties: `modResults` and `modRequest`.

#### `modResults`

The `modResults` object contains the data to modify and return. Its type depends on the mod that's being used.

#### `modRequest`

The `modRequest` object contains the following additional properties supplied by the mod compiler.

| Property | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `projectRoot` | `string` | Project root directory for the universal app. |
| `platformProjectRoot` | `string` | Project root for the specific platform. |
| `modName` | `string` | Name of the mod. |
| `platform` | `ModPlatform` | Name of the platform used in the mods config. |
| `projectName` | `string` | (iOS only) The path component used for querying project files. For example, `projectRoot/ios/[projectName]/`. |

## Create your own mod

For example, if you want to write a mod to update the Xcode Project's "product name", you'll create a config plugin file that uses the [`withXcodeProject`](https://docs.expo.dev/config-plugins/mods.md#ios) mod plugin.

```ts my-config-plugin.ts
import { ConfigPlugin, withXcodeProject, IOSConfig } from 'expo/config-plugins';

const withCustomProductName: ConfigPlugin<string> = (config, customName) => {
  return withXcodeProject(
    config,
    async (
      config
    ) => {
      config.modResults = IOSConfig.Name.setProductName({ name: customName }, config.modResults);
      return config;
    }
  );
};

// Usage:

/// Create a config
const config = {
  name: 'my app',
};

/// Use the plugin
export default withCustomProductName(config, 'new_name');
```

## Plugin module resolution

When implementing plugins, there are two fundamental approaches to consider:

1.  **Plugins defined within your app's project**: These plugins live locally within your project, making them easy to customize and maintain alongside your app's code. They are ideal for project-specific customizations.
    
2.  **Standalone package plugins**: These plugins exist as separate packages and are published to npm. This approach is ideal for reusable plugins that can be shared across multiple projects.
    

Both approaches provide the same capabilities for modifying your native configuration, but differ in how they're structured and imported. The sections below explain how module resolution works for each approach.

> Any resolution pattern that isn't specified below is unexpected behavior, and subject to breaking changes.

### Plugins defined within your app's project

With plugins defined within your app's project, you can implement plugins directly in your project in several ways:

#### File import

You can quickly create a plugin in your project by creating a JavaScript/TypeScript file and use it in your config like any other JS/TS file.

`app.config.ts``` `import "./my-config-plugin"` ``

`my-config-plugin.ts``✓ Imported from config`

In the above example, the config plugin file contains a bare minimum function:

```ts my-config-plugin.ts
module.exports = ({ config }: { config: ExpoConfig }) => {};
```

#### Inline function inside of dynamic app config

Expo config objects also support passing functions as-is to the `plugins` array. This is useful for testing, or if you want to use a plugin without creating a file.

```js app.config.ts
const withCustom = (config, props) => config;

const config = {
  plugins: [
    [
      withCustom,
      {
        /* props */
      },
    ],
    withCustom,
  ],
};
```

One caveat to using functions instead of strings is that serialization will replace the function with the function's name. This keeps **manifests** (kind of like the **index.html** for your app) working as expected. Here is what the serialized config would look like:

```json
{
  "plugins": [["withCustom", {}], "withCustom"]
}
```

### Standalone package plugins

> See [Create a module with a config plugin](https://docs.expo.dev/modules/config-plugin-and-native-module-tutorial.md) for a step-by-step guide on how to create a standalone package plugin.

Standalone package plugins can be implemented in two ways:

#### 1\. Dedicated config plugin packages

These are npm packages whose sole purpose is to provide a config plugin. For a dedicated config plugin package, you can export your plugin using `app.plugin.js`:

`app.config.ts``` `import "expo-splash-screen"` ``

#### 2\. Config plugins with companion packages

When a config plugin is part of a Node module without an **app.plugin.js**, it uses the package's `main` entry point:

`app.config.ts``` `import "expo-splash-screen"` ``

# UI architecture & research

## Design

GigaCode uses ink-navy surfaces, electric azure actions, icy cyan highlights and restrained glows in dark mode; light mode uses an ice-blue canvas, white chrome, navy text and darker blue actions. Shared semantic palettes live in `src/lib/palette.ts`, including syntax colors. `ThemeProvider` hydrates the persisted preference before showing route content, defaults to dark, survives navigation, and applies page background/color-scheme without reading browser globals during SSR. CodeMirror receives the mode as a serializable prop and reconfigures theme/highlight extensions live rather than remounting or inverting the editor.

Space Grotesk typography, rounded layered editor chrome and a static refractive blue lens keep the workspace cinematic without obstructing the code. Mobile web replaces the Files sidebar with a modal sheet and stacks editor/output; authentication becomes a single keyboard-aware column. All lens artwork is static and hidden from accessibility tools. The universal architecture remains intact; this iteration deliberately focuses on browser design and verification, not native builds.

## Boundaries and packages

- **Expo Router / React Native:** native navigation, safe areas, keyboard avoidance, forms, buttons, file library, and output. No web-only shell or parallel mobile UI.
- **`@uiw/react-codemirror` + `@codemirror/lang-python`:** mature editor behavior, parser-backed highlighting, indentation, built-in globals (including `print`), local variables, and snippets. `python()` registers both local and global completion sources; there is deliberately no hand-maintained completion dictionary. The button uses CodeMirror's `startCompletion` for touch access. Cmd/Ctrl shortcuts use CodeMirror keymaps.
- **Expo DOM component:** only `PythonEditor.tsx` begins with `'use dom'`. Web renders it directly; iOS/Android embed its bundle. SDK 57 uses the built-in `@expo/dom-webview`, so no additional native WebView dependency is needed. Explicit parent height and `dom.style.flex` size it on native. Props are serializable; function props are top-level async actions. File IDs accompany editor changes to protect against a delayed bridge event editing the newly selected file. CodeMirror mounts after hydration.
- **AsyncStorage:** working guest persistence without inventing an auth backend. A versioned Zod schema validates restored data; invalid data is not overwritten. The root provider survives route changes. Debounced autosave plus explicit Save share an ordered write queue to prevent stale writes. Save feedback is only shown after the storage promise resolves. Storage errors keep the in-memory edits and offer retry. If opening storage fails, editing is locked to avoid replacing existing data.
- **React Hook Form / Zod / resolvers:** cross-platform controlled inputs and shared validation. Sign-up password requirements are not imposed on sign-in. Credentials are never sent, logged, or persisted. The async service guard always rejects clearly; no fake session is produced.
- **Expo LinearGradient / vector icons / bundled Google font:** lightweight native-compatible visual primitives; no runtime font CDN or animation loop.

## Honest offline behavior

There is no Python interpreter, execution API, token store, or simulated network latency in this UI. Run creates a timestamped local explanation, not a Python result. There is no Stop button because there is no running request. Cloud Save is represented by the signed-out cloud-files panel and sign-in navigation, not a pretend save. Guest saves are explicitly device-local. The screen continues to offer guest editing while account services are absent.

## Future Python boundary (proposal, not an implemented API)

Keep backend implementation separate from the DOM editor. Choose the actual auth/session and execution sandbox design before wiring these client interactions:

| Proposed endpoint | Purpose / response |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /auth/signup` | Validated account creation; verification status, no assumed session |
| `POST /auth/login`, `GET /auth/me`, `POST /auth/logout` | Real session lifecycle; secure platform-appropriate session handling |
| `GET /files`, `POST /files`, `PATCH /files/:id` | Authenticated, user-scoped cloud Python files; stable ID, filename, code, revision, timestamps |
| `POST /executions` | Submit code to a separately sandboxed Python worker; execution ID / status |
| `GET /executions/:id`, `DELETE /executions/:id` | Bounded stdout/stderr, exit status, timeout, and actual cancellation |

When implemented, add a client adapter configured by `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL` (never secrets), response validation, abort/timeouts, typed HTTP errors, and a real loading/cancellation state. Use authenticated authorization for cloud files; do not silently upload local drafts. Never execute arbitrary Python inside the API process. This release deliberately does **not** consume that environment variable or send credentials to a configurable unverified endpoint.

## Research sources checked for this implementation

- [Expo SDK 57 reference](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v57.0.0/) - React Native / React versions and SDK-compatible package installation.
- [Expo documentation index](https://docs.expo.dev/llms.txt) - current API/documentation entry points.
- [Using React DOM in Expo native apps](https://docs.expo.dev/guides/dom-components/) (updated September 29, 2026) - SDK 56+ bundled WebView, async native actions, serialization, manual sizing, Expo Go support.
- [CodeMirror Python language source](https://github.com/codemirror/lang-python/blob/main/src/python.ts) - verified `python()` registers `localCompletionSource` and `globalCompletion`.

## Verification scope

Unit tests target validation, versioned draft restoration, filename rules, write ordering, storage retry, the unavailable account boundary, theme preference decoding and WCAG normal-text contrast for both palettes. `scripts/review-web.mts` uses development-only Playwright under Node (for reliable browser child-process handling on Windows) to check both modes at 390/768/1024/1440px, live syntax/cursor changes, suggestions, file operations, auth validation/offline notices, reload/route persistence, browser runtime errors and overflow. `bun run build` exports web only. No native build/export or device validation is included in this iteration. Before a future native release, test the editor's touch suggestions and soft-keyboard sizing on both iOS and Android; configure production icons, auth, and a sandboxed execution backend separately.

2. Fetch the matching versioned docs: `https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v<major>.0.0/`

## Navigation & Routing

- Use **Expo Router** for all navigation. Routes live in `src/app/` — every file there is a screen, `_layout.tsx` files define navigators. Keep non-route code (components, hooks, utils) outside `src/app/`.

- Docs: https://docs.expo.dev/router/introduction.md

## Building with EAS

Use EAS to build, sign, and submit the app in the cloud (`eas build`, `eas submit`) and to ship over-the-air updates (`eas update`) — no local Xcode or Android Studio required. - If `ios/` and `android/` directories do not exist, they are generated (Continuous Native Generation). Never create or edit them by hand — configure native behavior in `app.json` and config plugins.

185: - `FAILED` always means the user's program failed or the sandbox setup failed. It is final and is never retried.
186: - Infrastructure failures, such as a lease expiring, go back to `QUEUED` with a 5s, 20s or 60s backoff, until
187:   `attempt >= max_attempts`, at which point the job becomes `DEAD_LETTERED`.
188: 
189: ## Write path (`POST /v1/executions`)
190: 
191: 1. Authenticate with the session cookie plus CSRF, or with a Bearer API key, and load the tenant.
192: 2. Rate limit with a Redis token bucket at `max_exec_per_min`. If Redis is down, fall back to an in-memory bucket at
193:    half the rate per instance. Over the limit: `429` with `Retry-After`.
194: 3. Validate with zod: language, safe paths (no `..`, absolute paths, NUL or backslash), at most 20 files, source size
195:    against `max_source_bytes` (413 if over), stdin up to 256 KB, and limits through `resolveLimits`. Limits over a cap
196:    are rejected with 400 `limit_exceeded`, never silently clamped.
197: 4. Idempotency: the same key with the same `request_hash` returns the existing execution with 200. A different hash
198:    returns 409. A tenant with 200 queued jobs gets 429 `queue_full`.
199: 5. Insert the `CREATED` row and its event.
200: 6. Upload the files, stdin and finally `manifest.json` to S3, with retries. If the upload still fails, transition to
201:    `FAILED` (`artifact_upload_failed`) and return 503.
202: 7. Transition `CREATED → QUEUED`, publish `queue:wake`, and return `202 {id, status}`.
203: 
204: Concurrency quotas are enforced at claim time, not on submit.
205: 
206: ## Worker execution path (one slot)
207: 
208: 1. **Claim:** call `worker_claim`. If there's nothing to do, sleep for a jittered poll interval, or wake early on
209:    `queue:wake`.
210: 2. **Heartbeat** every `HEARTBEAT_SECONDS`:
211:    - If the lease was lost, abort the sandbox and discard the result.
212:    - If `cancel_requested` is set, abort and complete as `CANCELLED`.
213: 3. **Start:** `DISPATCHED→STARTING`.
214:    - Create `/var/lib/worker/runs/{id}-{attempt}` with mode 0711. When the worker runs as root, the workspace inside
215:      it is a per-run 128 MB tmpfs owned by the slot's sandbox uid.
216:    - Download the manifest and the files, and verify each file's size and sha256.
217:    - If the source is missing or corrupt, stop heartbeating and leave the job to lease expiry. That is an
218:      infrastructure failure, so it is retried.
219: 4. **Run:** `STARTING→RUNNING`. C and C++ compile first (wall 10s, memory 512 MB). A compile failure becomes
220:    `FAILED/compile_error` with the compiler output as stderr. Then the program runs with the tenant's limits.
221: 5. **Upload:** put stdout, stderr and `result.json` under `attempts/{n}/`, with retries. If the upload still fails,
222:    stop heartbeating and leave the job to lease expiry.
223: 6. **Complete (fenced):** call `worker_complete`. If it returns false, delete this attempt's S3 prefix and increment
224:    `metrics:fenced_results_discarded_total`.
225: 7. **Cleanup** in `finally`: kill the run's cgroup, unmount the workspace tmpfs, and remove the run directory.
226: 
227: Result mapping (`apps/worker/src/result-mapping.ts`), most specific cause first:
228: 
229: | Cause | Status | `failure_reason` |
230: |---|---|---|
231: | Cancelled | `CANCELLED` | — |
232: | Sandbox setup error | `FAILED` | `sandbox_setup_error` |
233: | Wall time exceeded | `TIMEOUT` | — |
234: | cgroup `oom_kill` | `FAILED` | `oom` |
235: | SIGSYS (seccomp) | `FAILED` | `seccomp_violation` |
236: | Compile failed | `FAILED` | `compile_error` |
237: | Exit 0 | `SUCCESS` | — |
238: | Killed by a signal | `FAILED` | `killed_by_signal` |
239: | Any other non-zero exit | `FAILED` | `runtime_error` |
240: 
241: ## Sandbox (`packages/sandbox`)
242: 
243: `NsjailDriver` renders a protobuf-text config for each run (`nsjail-config.ts`, using nsjail 3.4 field names) and a
244: kafel policy (`seccomp.ts`, combining `base.kafel` with an optional per-language addition). It then runs:
245: 
246: ```
247: /bin/sh -c 'echo $$ > "$1" && shift && exec "$@"' sh <cgroup.procs> nsjail --config <file>
248: ```
249: 
250: The wrapper script is a constant. Every value is passed as argv, never interpolated into shell text. The wrapper puts
251: nsjail and all of its descendants into a **cgroup that the worker owns** (`cgroup.ts`: memory.max, memory.swap.max=0,
252: pids.max and cpu.max). That lets the worker read `memory.peak`, `memory.events` (`oom_kill`) and `cpu.stat`, and kill
253: every descendant with `cgroup.kill`.
254: 
255: Wall time is enforced twice: nsjail's `time_limit` (rounded up to whole seconds), and a worker watchdog that fires
256: after the wall limit plus 1.5s. stdout and stderr go through pipes into files capped at 1 MB each. Output beyond the
257: cap is drained and discarded so the program can't block on a full pipe.
258: 
259: `DockerDriver` is the dev-only fallback for machines without nsjail. It uses `docker run --network none --read-only
260: --cap-drop ALL …`, refuses to construct when `NODE_ENV=production`, and the worker prints a "DEV ONLY" warning when it
261: is selected.
262: 
263: ## Read path
264: 
265: - `GET /v1/executions/:id`: checks the Redis cache, then the read replica (`DATABASE_READ_URL`), falling back to the
266:   primary.
267: - `GET /v1/executions`: a cursor-paginated list.
268: - `/logs`: a 60s presigned URL, or `?inline=true` to stream up to 1 MB as text/plain with an `X-Truncated` header.
269: - `/result`: the parsed `result.json`.
270: - `/source`: used by the dashboard's Re-run button.
271: - `/events`: SSE, cookie sessions only. Sends the current state, then pushes updates from Redis pub/sub with a 2s
272:   polling fallback and a `: ping` every 15s, and closes on a terminal state.
273: - `/cancel`: transitions `QUEUED → CANCELLED`; for an active job it sets `cancel_requested` and returns 202.
274: - Other tenants' ids return `404`.
275: 
276: ## Known limitations
277: 
278: - **TCB:** the host kernel is part of the trusted computing base. A kernel bug reachable through the allowed syscalls
279:   could break isolation. Future work is gVisor or Firecracker microVMs.
280: - **Dev compose privileges:** the compose `worker` runs `privileged: true` with a private cgroup namespace, so nsjail
281:   can create namespaces and manage cgroups inside Docker Desktop. A production worker runs as a systemd service on a
282:   dedicated VM (`infra/worker-vm/`).
283: - **Worker runs as root.** It needs to set arbitrary uid maps, mount per-run tmpfs and write cgroups. User code never
284:   runs as root; it runs as uid 65534, mapped to host uid 200000+slot, with no capabilities and `no_new_privs`.
285: - **tsx in images:** the API and worker images run TypeScript through `tsx` instead of compiled JS, and install dev
286:   dependencies.
287: - **Unpinned MinIO:** `cgr.dev/chainguard/minio:latest` is used for local S3 because Docker Hub no longer serves
288:   `minio/minio`. It cannot be pinned on the free tier.
289: - **Exit codes above 128:** nsjail reports a signalled child as exit code 128+N, so the driver maps exit codes 129–192
290:   to signals. A program that calls `exit(137)` itself is reported as killed by SIGKILL.
291: - **Whole-second time limit:** nsjail's `time_limit` is in whole seconds. Sub-second precision comes only from the
292:   measured `wallMs` and the watchdog, which fires at the wall limit plus 1.5s.
293: - **Node RLIMIT_AS:** Node gets a 16 GB address-space rlimit because V8 reserves large virtual ranges at startup.
294:   Other runtimes get 4×memory+1 GB. cgroup `memory.max` is the effective memory limit.
295: - **DockerDriver:** OOM is inferred from exit code 137 without a timeout, there are no CPU or peak-memory stats, and
296:   workspace paths must be valid on the docker host.
297: - **Run directory mode:** per-run directories are mode 0711, not the 0700 in the spec, because nsjail bind-mounts the
298:   workspace from inside the new user namespace, which needs search permission on the parent directories.
299: - **Single instances:** one Postgres primary (optional read replica) and one Redis; no clustering. Autoscaling is
300:   documented ([RUNBOOK.md](RUNBOOK.md)), not implemented.
301: - **API DB role:** the API connects as the database owner (a superuser in the dev compose). Only workers use the
302:   restricted `worker_role`.
303: - **Worker transitions:** worker-side transitions run in SQL functions, not through the TypeScript
304:   `transitionExecution`, so the allowed worker transitions are encoded twice: once in `states.ts` and once in the SQL.
305: - **Wake-up hint:** the `queue:wake` hint wakes only one waiting slot per worker process (`Hints.waitForWork` keeps a
306:   single waiter). The other slots fall back to polling, which stays the source of truth.
307: - **IMDSv2:** IMDSv2 with hop limit 1 has to be set through the cloud API. `setup.sh` only documents the command.
308: - **Seccomp profile:** the kafel policy was built for Python 3.12, Node 20 and GCC 13 on x86_64 and validated by the
309:   self-test and the abuse suite. A different runtime version may need policy additions.

# GigaCode architecture — viva guide

**GigaCode is a multi-tenant platform for running user-submitted code.** The Expo app and web dashboard let users write code, submit it, and see the output. The code runs on a **separate Linux worker inside a sandbox**, not on the phone, in the browser, or inside the API server.

## Your 60-second opening answer

> “GigaCode separates the **control plane** from the **execution plane**. The control plane is a Fastify API that authenticates users, validates requests, enforces tenant limits, and manages job state. When a user presses Run, the API stores the source in S3-compatible object storage, queues the job in PostgreSQL, and returns an execution ID immediately. A Linux worker claims the job and runs it inside an nsjail sandbox with resource limits and networking disabled by default. The worker uploads the output to object storage and records the final status in PostgreSQL. The client gets status and results through the API. Redis is used for caching, rate limiting, and notifications, but PostgreSQL is the durable source of truth.”

## Diagram to draw on the board

```text
Expo app / Web dashboard / API client
                  │  HTTPS
                  ▼
             Fastify API
         submit │     │ read status / logs
                ▼     │
       PostgreSQL ◄────┘       Redis
       queue + job state       cache + notifications
                ▲
                │ worker claims jobs
                ▼
           Linux worker ────── S3 / MinIO
                │              source, logs, results
                ▼
          nsjail sandbox
          runs user code
```

The API also writes the original source to S3/MinIO. **Clients never connect directly to workers.**

## What happens when you press Run?

1. **Submit.** The Expo app sends source code, optional input, and execution limits to `POST /v1/executions`.
2. **Validate and queue.** The API checks authentication, tenant quotas, and input. It creates a job record, uploads the source, marks the job `QUEUED`, and returns `202 Accepted` with an execution ID. **Accepted does not mean finished.**
3. **Claim and execute.** An available worker slot claims the job in a database transaction. The worker downloads the source, starts an isolated sandbox, and captures stdout, stderr, and exit status.
4. **Store and display.** The worker uploads the artifacts and records a terminal state such as `SUCCESS`, `FAILED`, or `TIMEOUT`. The Expo app polls the API for the result; the web dashboard can use server-sent events for status updates.

```text
CREATED → QUEUED → DISPATCHED → STARTING → RUNNING → SUCCESS
                                              └──→ FAILED / TIMEOUT / CANCELLED
```

## Likely viva questions

| Question | Answer you can give |
|---|---|
| **Why not execute code in the API?** | User code is untrusted and can take a long time or consume too many resources. Separating execution keeps the API responsive and puts the code on an isolated worker. |
| **Why use both PostgreSQL and Redis?** | PostgreSQL stores the durable queue and authoritative job state. Redis makes caching, rate limiting, and notifications faster. If a Redis wake-up is missed, workers still poll PostgreSQL. |
| **How do two workers avoid claiming the same job?** | PostgreSQL uses `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` during the claim transaction. A worker locks the row it claims, so other workers skip that row instead of also taking it. |
| **What if a worker crashes halfway through?** | A claim is a **lease**: the worker must renew it with heartbeats. If it expires, the reaper requeues the job or marks it dead-lettered when attempts are exhausted. An old worker cannot commit a result after losing its lease. That protects the final result; it does not promise exactly-once execution. |
| **How is the sandbox isolated?** | Linux **namespaces** restrict what the process can see, **cgroups** limit resources such as CPU, memory, and process count, and **seccomp** restricts system calls. The sandbox still shares the host kernel, so it is **not** a VM. |
| **What does multi-tenant mean?** | Different users or teams share the same platform, but authorization, job data, and quotas are scoped to their tenant. One tenant cannot read another tenant’s execution through the normal API. |
| **Does it autoscale?** | **Not automatically.** Each worker has a configured number of concurrent slots. More worker instances can be deployed, but there is no controller that adds workers when the queue grows. |
| **Is `/simulation` actually a simulator?** | It’s a Breakscale-inspired monitoring view with optional bounded real test traffic. It shows polled **tenant-level** queue and execution activity, not simulated predictions or actual fleet-wide CPU utilization. |

**Best demo sequence:** Open the Expo editor → run `print("Hello, viva")` → show the output and execution history → point at the diagram and explain where the source, job state, and output are stored. The distinction to remember is: **PostgreSQL owns job state, S3 stores files, Redis speeds things up, and the Linux worker runs the code.**

content.text: **Choosing C++**

I’d show these four demos in this order: **Python with custom input → C++ compilation → runtime error → timeout**. Each shows a different part of GigaCode, and none needs external libraries or internet access.

## 1. Python — grade report with custom input

Select **Python**, paste this code, and enter `78 85 92` in the **Standard input (stdin)** field.

```python
marks = list(map(int, input().split()))
average = sum(marks) / len(marks)

print(f"Subjects: {len(marks)}")
print(f"Average: {average:.2f}")
print("Result:", "PASS" if min(marks) >= 40 else "FAIL")
```

Expected output:

```text
Subjects: 3
Average: 85.00
Result: PASS
```

**Say:** “The app sends the source and input to the API. A worker runs it remotely and returns the output.” If the examiner asks for a different input, change one mark to `35` and run it again.

## 2. C++ — compile and run binary search

Select **C++** and paste this into `main.cpp`.

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> values{42, 7, 19, 3, 12};
    std::sort(values.begin(), values.end());

    const int target = 19;
    bool found = std::binary_search(values.begin(), values.end(), target);

    std::cout << target << (found ? " found\n" : " not found\n");
}
```

**Expected:** `19 found` and status `SUCCESS`.

**Say:** “For C++, the worker compiles the source first, then runs the compiled program. The phone doesn’t need a compiler.”

## 3. Python — show stdout and stderr on failure

```python
print("Starting calculation...", flush=True)
total = 120
count = 0
print(total / count)
```

**Expected:** `FAILED`, with `Starting calculation...` in **stdout** and a `ZeroDivisionError` traceback in **stderr**.

**Say:** “A bug in the submitted program fails that execution, not the API. We still get the output produced before the error and the traceback.”

## 4. Python — show the execution timeout

Set the execution timeout to **2 seconds** (`2000` ms if the field uses milliseconds), then run:

```python
import time

print("Job started", flush=True)
time.sleep(8)
print("This line should not appear")
```

**Expected:** `TIMEOUT`. The first line should appear, but the last one shouldn’t.

**Say:** “Even though the program is sleeping and barely using CPU, the worker enforces a **wall-clock limit** and stops it.”

**Before the viva:** Save the snippets as drafts and try all four once on the exact device and server you’ll use. Finish by opening **History** and pointing out `SUCCESS`, `FAILED`, and `TIMEOUT` side by side—that shows GigaCode tracks execution outcomes, not just printed output.

**Setting benchmark parameters**

Show the examiner **four sandbox controls**, not four algorithms. For each demo, run **the same Python code twice and change only one setting**. That makes it clear GigaCode is enforcing the limit, not the program. Use a demo tenant and turn on per-run resource measurements in **Run Settings**.

## 1. RAM — show the sandbox stopping a memory-heavy job

Run at **256 MiB**, then at **64 MiB**. Set the timeout to **5 seconds**.

```python
blocks = []

for used in range(8, 97, 8):
    block = bytearray(8 * 1024 * 1024)

    # Touch every page so the allocation actually uses RAM.
    for offset in range(0, len(block), 4096):
        block[offset] = 1

    blocks.append(block)
    print(f"Allocated {used} MiB", flush=True)

print("Finished")
```

**Show:** At 256 MiB, it reaches `Finished`. At 64 MiB, expect it to stop before that, commonly with `FAILED` / `oom`. It can stop before printing `64 MiB` because the Python runtime itself also uses memory.

**Say:** “The memory limit applies to the whole sandbox, not just my array.”

## 2. CPU — show throttling, not termination

Run at **100% CPU allowance**, then **20%**. Keep the timeout at **5 seconds** for both.

```python
import time

start = time.monotonic()
cpu_start = time.process_time()
iterations = 0

while time.monotonic() - start < 2:
    iterations += 1

print(f"Wall time: {time.monotonic() - start:.2f} s")
print(f"CPU time:  {time.process_time() - cpu_start:.2f} s")
print(f"Iterations: {iterations:,}")
```

**Show:** Both runs take about two seconds of wall time. At 20%, expect **less CPU time and fewer iterations**.

**Say:** “CPU quota limits how much work the program can do per second. It doesn’t kill the program. The wall-clock timeout is a separate control.”

## 3. Internet — show outbound access blocked

Set the timeout to **5 seconds**. Run with **Program internet access Off**. If your demo deployment permits egress, run it again with **On**.

```python
from urllib.request import urlopen

print("Trying one HTTPS request...", flush=True)

try:
    with urlopen("https://example.com", timeout=2) as response:
        print("HTTP status:", response.status)
except OSError as error:
    print("Request failed:", error)
```

**Show:** With access off, expect no HTTP response. With access on, expect `HTTP status: 200` **if the worker can reach that site**. Rehearse the on case first: DNS or deployment rules can also block it.

**Say:** “The app can still contact our API. It’s the submitted program inside the sandbox that can’t reach the internet.”

## 4. Threads — show new threads being refused

Under **Processes / threads**, run at **16**, then **4**. This tries to start just eight threads and keeps them alive together so they count toward the limit.

```python
import threading

release = threading.Event()
workers = []

try:
    for number in range(1, 9):
        worker = threading.Thread(target=release.wait)
        try:
            worker.start()
        except RuntimeError as error:
            print(f"Thread {number} refused: {error}", flush=True)
            break
        workers.append(worker)
finally:
    release.set()
    for worker in workers:
        worker.join()

print(f"Started {len(workers)} of 8 threads")
```

**Show:** At 16, expect `Started 8 of 8 threads`. At 4, expect fewer threads and a refusal message. The main thread and any other sandbox tasks count too, so don’t promise exactly four successful starts. The run can still show `SUCCESS` because the script handles the refusal.

**Best viva closing line:** “These limits behave differently: RAM can kill the job, CPU throttles it, network isolation blocks the connection, and the task limit refuses new threads. The same code behaves differently when I change the sandbox policy.”

The program **never ran**. The online editor is compiling `main.c` in **C++ mode** while passing `-std=c17`, a flag that only works in **C mode**.

If the editor lets you change the compiler settings, select **C** rather than C++, or use `clang -x c -std=c17 main.c -o demo` on a Linux machine you control.

For the viva, run this demo in **GigaCode with C selected**, on your own nsjail worker. Even if the online editor compiles it, it may use WebAssembly or a different sandbox, so its output won’t verify GigaCode’s policy. The result you want to show is **`FAILED` with `seccomp_violation`** and only the `Before` line—not `Compilation failed`.

For your GigaCode viva, **use the harmless syscall probe, not a real reboot command**. Your code has a typo: `OUL` starts with the letter **O**. Use `0UL` (zero) instead:

```c
syscall(SYS_reboot, 0UL, 0UL, 0UL, NULL);
```

Run it in **C mode on your own GigaCode Linux worker**, not a third-party playground. The deliberately invalid arguments ensure the call cannot reboot the machine. If GigaCode reports **`seccomp_violation`** and the `After` line never appears, you’ve demonstrated that the sandbox stopped the job at the syscall. If `After` appears, the syscall returned an error instead—that’s a different result.

If you actually need to restart a machine you administer, use its normal **Restart** control rather than code submitted to a sandbox.

messages.text: i think most online c compilers has protection against it why

content.text:
Yes. Online C playgrounds run **untrusted code from many users**. If one program could reboot a shared server, it could interrupt everyone’s work. The protection usually comes from **the environment that runs the program**, not the C compiler.

Different services enforce it in different ways:

- **Browser-based runners** may compile to WebAssembly. The program doesn’t have direct access to Linux system calls.
- **Linux runners** typically run code without administrative privileges, so a privileged operation can return `Operation not permitted`.
- **Sandboxed runners** can use a syscall filter such as **seccomp** to terminate the program before the operation is attempted. That’s what your GigaCode demo is meant to show.

Your screenshot showed a **compiler configuration error** (`-std=c17` used in C++ mode), so the program never ran. That’s different from a sandbox block.

**Viva line:** “Compiling a call isn’t the same as authorizing it. The compiler translates the code; the operating system and sandbox decide what it can do.”
